{"id": "53:23/q14", "question": "What desire or 'souls' does the verse mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q14/p1", "position": "It is personal appetite and whim, especially the appealing practice of idol worship and hoped-for intercession.", "reasons": "Dāmghānī glosses hawā as lust, comparing 20:16, 28:50, 7:176, 25:43 and 46:23, and nufūs as hearts, comparing 12:53. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi say Satan made the practice attractive. Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan distinguish pleasure from reason's good outcome; al-Biqaʿi says deficient souls pull downward and intellect upward. Al-Razi says plural souls are distributive. Bursevi calls them evil-commanding selves. Islahi calls the desired thing a polytheistic innovation that evades reality's demands; Kuranyolu sees subjective religious motives. Study Quran compares capricious wandering at 45:23 and the evil-commanding soul at 12:53, and notes the literal rendering 'what their souls fancy.'"}]}
{"id": "53:23/q15", "question": "Are all conjecture and desire condemned?", "turns_on": "The availability of evidence and whether attraction is grounded in it; the notes distinguish creed, law, social judgment, and sound love.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q15/p1", "position": "Foundational religious claims require evidence and certainty; probable judgment may be proper elsewhere.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says conjecture in religion's foundations is unsound. Al-Razi cites 'I am as My servant thinks of Me' as a seeming counterexample, then allows preponderant probability when certainty cannot be reached; here guidance made certainty available. Al-Qushayri and al-Biqaʿi distinguish good opinion of God and uncertainty over one's fate from speculation about God, attributes and rulings. Ibn ʿAshur distinguishes foundational belief from branches of law, and praiseworthy from blameworthy social conjecture, citing 49:12 and a saying urging vigilance."}, {"id": "53:23/q15/p2", "position": "Love supported by evidence is not the appetite blamed here.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur says the restriction to appetite alone carries the blame; evidence can deepen love of something true. He cites prophetic praise of mutual love for God and attachment to mosques, and the Prophet's delight in prayer."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q16", "question": "How does the clause about guidance connect syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause describes their condition while following conjecture or interrupts the sentence before 53:24.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q16/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial: they follow conjecture even while guidance has come.", "reasons": "Al-Samin, al-Alusi, Ibn ʿAshur and al-Tabatabaʾi use this parse; the conflict intensifies blame and wonder. Bursevi says either parse exposes conjecture's falsity."}, {"id": "53:23/q16/p2", "position": "It is parenthetical, interrupting the rebuke before the following question.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Samin describe an insertion; al-Samin says 53:24 resumes with disjunctive am understood as bal plus interrogative hamza. He reports al-Zamakhshari that the question denies people's possession of whatever they wish. Al-Alusi and Bursevi also allow the parenthesis."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q17", "question": "What guidance came from their Lord?", "turns_on": "Which concrete medium of divine guidance is meant: Book, Messenger, both, or also miracles.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q17/p1", "position": "The Qur'an or revealed Book.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Dāmghānī, al-Burhan and al-Itqan give this gloss; Dāmghānī compares 18:55 and 17:94. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi list the Book as an alternative to the Messenger; al-Alusi says the Qur'an can be called the guide or emphatically 'guidance.'"}, {"id": "53:23/q17/p2", "position": "The Messenger, Muhammad, and his religious law or clarification.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz, Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Qurtubi identify Muhammad or his teaching; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi offer the Messenger as an alternative. Al-Qurtubi specifies the clarification that idols are not gods."}, {"id": "53:23/q17/p3", "position": "The Book and Messenger together, clarifying exclusive worship of God.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Nahhas, al-Wahidi al-Basit, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi, al-Biqaʿi, Bursevi, Elmalılı and Islahi name both. Al-Tabari says God alone is worshipped, the One who prevails; al-Nahhas calls idol worship associationism and unbelief. Islahi includes Sunnah and links the surah's opening praise of revelation."}, {"id": "53:23/q17/p4", "position": "The Qur'an, messengers, or miracles can each be meant.", "reasons": "Al-Razi gives this range of possible referents."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q18", "question": "What is stressed by the wording about guidance from 'their Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q18/p1", "position": "Clear, complete guidance makes their persistence especially astonishing and disobedient.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan express wonder that evidence did not stop worship. Ibn ʿAshur says the oath-like lām insists that convincing guidance truly came, 'their Lord' stresses rebellion against their Creator, and the definite article marks completeness and clarity. Al-Biqaʿi says reason required acceptance even through an enemy."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q19", "question": "Did those addressed benefit from the guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q19/p1", "position": "No; they turned from clear guidance and continued worship, conjecture and wishful hope.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says they did not benefit. Al-Qushayri, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Elmalılı say they abandoned revelation despite proof; Islahi compares following conjecture in daylight to leaping into death. Al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi call their persistence astonishing."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q20", "question": "What does the passage teach about evidence, inquiry, and human responsibility?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q20/p1", "position": "Religious claims must be argued from acquired knowledge, and God has removed excuse by giving guidance and capacity.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says the argument with unbelievers validates religious debate and shows knowledge is acquired. He says God furnished proof, explanation and empowerment; people turned away themselves, opposing the coercion claim that God created their unbelief and withheld capacity. Kuranyolu says claims about God's attributes and lordship need direct contact or an authorized messenger; pagans claimed neither and rational scrutiny reveals their failure."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q21", "question": "What limit does the verse place on naming God or divine beings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q21/p1", "position": "People cannot invent divine names whose implications diminish God without revealed warrant.", "reasons": "Al-Razi answers the daughter claim: even if angels were considered directly from God, an offspring title implies deficiency. He says such names require revelation, citing 39:56; conventional naming is acceptable only when its benefit outweighs harm, and neither revelation nor reason supports these labels."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q22", "question": "What is the verse's inward warning about conjectural knowledge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q22/p1", "position": "Spiritual seekers can mistake conjecture and mental images for direct knowledge of God.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami and Bursevi report Junayd seeing seventy gnostics perish through imagining they knew God; Bursevi adds 39:67 and the limits of human capacity. Al-Wasiti says even Abu Yazid died in this delusion. Al-Baqlī warns that conceited claimants misread egoistic and satanic images as unveilings or divine lights: the Real exceeds shapes, and true vision belongs to saints. Al-Qushayri urges certainty and verification until knowledge is immediate; Shibli says realizing the Real's reality is that reality."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q23", "question": "What do the inward readings say the idolaters fail to see?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q23/p1", "position": "Their sensual selves and illusion-clouded minds mistake imagined forms for realities and miss divine manifestation in creation.", "reasons": "Al-Najmiyya says created things have no independent power to create, destroy, benefit or harm; beings manifest divine names and beauty or majesty, while the Perfect Human manifests these fully and is God's vicegerent. It says idolaters descend into animal desire and bodily darkness rather than perceiving spiritual realities, comparing 53:28. Bursevi says they squander innate readiness for the Prophet, Qur'an, miracles and signs by adopting animal and elemental traits."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q24", "question": "How does an inward account relate earthly guidance to pre-eternal light?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q24/p1", "position": "Guidance comes in earthly life, while a person lacking God's pre-eternal light remains without light.", "reasons": "Bursevi makes this distinction in his inward reading."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q25", "question": "Where was al-ʿUzzā's shrine, and who founded it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q25/p1", "position": "It stood at Hirād in Nakhlah al-Shāmiyya, opposite al-Ghumayr on the Iraq road, and Zālim ibn Asʿad first built it.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi gives the location as nine miles beyond Dhat ʿIrq toward al-Bustan."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q26", "question": "What were al-ʿUzzā's shrine building and slaughter site called?", "turns_on": "The notes identify different parts of the sanctuary, the shrine house and its sacrificial place.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q26/p1", "position": "The shrine building was a bas, meaning a house.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi gives this gloss."}, {"id": "53:23/q26/p2", "position": "Its slaughtering site was al-Ghabghab, where meat from offerings was shared.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi says a Hudhali satire describes taking

{"id": "53:23/q27", "question": "How did Quraysh and other Arabs honor al-ʿUzzā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q27/p1", "position": "They used its name, visited, sacrificed, made offerings and oaths, and treated its precinct as sacred.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi says Quraysh counted it their greatest idol, named people ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā and heard a voice at its shrine. They guarded Siqām to imitate the Kaaba's sanctuary; Abu Jundub's poem attests its protected branches. Dirham ibn Zayd swears by al-ʿUzzā and God at Sarif. Al-Kalbi also reports the Prophet recalling a tawny camel offering while following his people's religion."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q28", "question": "What invocation of the goddesses is reported from pagan worship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q28/p1", "position": "Quraysh called al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt exalted gharānīq, God's daughters and hoped-for intercessors while circumambulating.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi reports the formula; Elmalılı cites Yaqut that it was pagan speech before Muhammad and describes a poetic comparison of white stones with high-flying birds."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q29", "question": "What does gharānīq mean in the reported formula?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q29/p1", "position": "It denotes high-flying white water birds, also figuratively a beautiful young woman or soft wind-stirred hair.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives gurnûk/gurneyk, a long-necked bird larger than a goose; the alternate senses vary by context."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q30", "question": "Was the gharānīq praise part of the Prophet's recitation?", "turns_on": "The report's transmission and whether pagan wording was mistakenly attributed to the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q30/p1", "position": "Some exegetes report that Satan inserted it, and God subsequently removed it and confirmed revelation.", "reasons": "Elmalılı attributes this report to some exegetes including al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari, linking it to 22:52."}, {"id": "53:23/q30/p2", "position": "The insertion report is fabricated or unestablished.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports Abu Hayyan's statement that Ibn Ishaq called it a heretical fabrication and wrote against it. He reports al-Bayhaqi's objections: criticized transmitters and absence from sound collections."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q31", "question": "If the disputed gharānīq words were spoken, how would this verse frame them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q31/p1", "position": "They would be a quotation of pagan speech immediately refuted as empty names.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says placement after the rebuke would form a coherent quotation, whereas inserting the formula directly after Manat disrupts the cadence. He says 53:26 already rejects hoped-for intercession even without a quotation."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q32", "question": "What are the reported pause forms of Manāt?", "turns_on": "Whether reports about spelling were mistaken for recitation, and whether the pause is with hāʾ or tāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q32/p1", "position": "Every reader pauses with hāʾ in accordance with the written form.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari rejects al-Ahwazi's all-tāʾ report and states this universal hāʾ reading."}, {"id": "53:23/q32/p2", "position": "Al-Kisāʾī alone pauses with hāʾ; other readers use tāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari rejects the Iraqi report as a confusion of Nusayr's spelling report with recitation."}, {"id": "53:23/q32/p3", "position": "All readers pause with tāʾ, and codices spell Manāt with wāw.", "reasons": "Al-Ahwazi is reported by Ibn al-Jazari, who rejects this and asserts hāʾ according to the writing."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q33", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding argument about intercession?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q33/p1", "position": "It rejects imagined intercession and prepares the warning that wishes cannot override God's judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says the following passage rebukes hoped-for idol intercession; Elmalılı points to 53:26 on angels' ineffectual intercession. Asad calls goddess and angel mediation wishful thinking and says analogous patterns persist in saint veneration and deification. Islahi says reward, punishment and God's control of heaven and earth are real, so wishes cannot save them; their imagined deities cannot avert Judgment. Al-Samin reports al-Zamakhshari that the next question denies obtaining whatever one wishes."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q34", "question": "What role does the verse play in the sūrah's larger argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q34/p1", "position": "It rebuts pagan worship after establishing revelation, and exposes ignorance and conjecture behind claims of intercession.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi says this section follows proof of prophecy based on monotheism and leads toward resurrection and recompense. Study Quran calls it the second section's reproach of Quraysh. Islahi says self-claimed deities cannot avert Judgment. Kuranyolu says Quraysh's idols illustrate historic deviations that enslave people to created things."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q35", "question": "How do the preceding male and female argument and its wording lead into this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q35/p1", "position": "The prior charge of an unjust division leads to a broader rejection of the names themselves.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur says even imagined injustice reveals belief and conduct. He analyzes ḍīzā as perhaps noun or verbal noun, though adjective is likelier; Sībawayh says an initial-kasra fuʿlā adjective is unattested. He records the majority's quiescent yāʾ and Ibn Kathir's hamza, reflecting the original verb. He also offers an analysis where afaraʾaytum is suspended from taking an object by the following negative inna, with the intervening male/female clause parenthetical. Kuranyolu cites 16:58-59 and 43:17-19 for the contradiction of preferring sons while assigning despised daughters to God."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q36", "question": "What kind of concision does 'they follow only conjecture and desire' exemplify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q36/p1", "position": "It exemplifies qasr, concise expression that compresses meaning without an omitted word.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani contrasts qasr with recoverable deletion and says judging where it works is subtler. He compares other compact Qur'anic statements about retribution as life, every shout, unattainable booty, desire, self-aggression and evil plotting. Bint al-Shati reports his distinction and his separate account that ellipsis can let the reader supply possibilities, citing 42:51 and 39:73."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q37", "question": "What illustrations warn against taking impressive names or appearances for realities?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q37/p1", "position": "A favorable name or human appearance can conceal the opposite reality.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes Jami's satire of calling a ruined thing prosperity and mistaking a swelling for fat; another poem likens apparently human people to predators or wolves in clothing."}]}
{"id": "53:23/q38", "question": "How is 'guidance came to them' read?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted direct address is plural or singular.", "positions": [{"id": "53:23/q38/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās read 'guidance came to you' in the plural.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya reports this direct-address variant."}, {"id": "53:23/q38/p2", "position": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports their reading as singular 'guidance came to you.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya attributes the alternative singular wording to al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q01", "question": "What reaches the limit of their knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether 'that' points to worldly life or preference, angel claims, conjecture, rejection, or turning away; and whether ʿilm denotes genuine knowledge, conjecture, or the known object.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q01/p1", "position": "Worldly livelihood, affairs, and pleasures exhaust what they know; they do not know religion or the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj links their worldly livelihood to 53:29 and says they cast aside the afterlife. Ibn ʿAṭiyya names farming, crafts, and deceptive status seeking. Abū Ḥayyān adds trades and cites 30:7. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī depicts a metaphorical endpoint: knowledge stops at the world, which then absorbs desire, concern, and hope. Islahi says they see outward appearances rather than deeper reality; the evident Creator makes a merely playful universe implausible, and 30:7 supplies the contrast. Al-Ṭabrisī calls immediate pleasure an animal-like aim unworthy of reason. The Study Quran contrasts religion. Bursevī and Ālūsī include false conjectural perception within ʿilm. Asad glosses the total extent or goal of knowledge."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p2", "position": "Preferring transient worldly life over the lasting Hereafter is their intellectual limit.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ links the angel claim with belittling their choice; al-Naḥḥās mentions fading adornment and status versus lasting reward. Jishumī says worldly benefit displaces lasting reward in ignorance. Rāzī relates this possibility to 53:29. Bursevī cites Bahr al-ʿUlūm and al-Irshād for choosing the world and restricting desire to it. Ālūsī prefers the contextual world over turning away or conjecture."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p3", "position": "Their claims that angels are God's daughters and intercessors mark their limit.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they rely on this and ignore the Qur'an. Al-Ṭabarī calls it shirk and uncertain conjecture. Al-Qurṭubī's alternative includes idols as alleged daughters. The Study Quran adds caprice and desire."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p4", "position": "Their furthest intellectual reach is conjecture or opinion itself.", "reasons": "Mujāhid calls it th

Al-Ṭabarī and the Study Quran relate conjecture to the angel claims."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p5", "position": "Their limit is rejecting the Messenger and God's revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls them people of shirk plotting against revelation; al-Naḥḥās adds obstinacy. Rāzī says ignorance followed their own withdrawal from remembrance, making punishment just despite the objection that God does not burden a child or mad person. He ranks responses to the Qur'an: wholehearted acceptance, accepting its miracle and following the Messenger, hesitation like Abū Ṭālib's, and blameful rejection."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p6", "position": "The demonstrative points to turning away; 'knowledge' may mean the known object, the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this third possibility from 53:29. Ālūsī rejects turning away as the antecedent. Al-Burhān explains that a verbal noun can carry passive force: ʿilm is the known thing, as ṣunʿ is the made thing."}, {"id": "53:30/q01/p7", "position": "The phrase names the extent of knowledge without specifying its subject.", "reasons": "Bursevī calls mablagh a place or extent noun. Asad gives 'total extent or goal.' Al-Burhān explains the passive sense of ʿilm. Al-Biqāʿī calls the assertion sarcastic because blindness to the afterlife leaves no real knowledge."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q02", "question": "Why describe their knowledge in these terms?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis is on belittling ignorance or confirming confined ambition.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q02/p1", "position": "The wording belittles narrow minds blind to the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ calls their judgment small and foolish; al-Biqāʿī calls the claim sarcastic because the afterlife is the root of knowledge. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the parenthesis belittles understanding. Islahi says temporary pleasure, timidity, and deprivation divert them from the eternal kingdom, citing 30:7."}, {"id": "53:30/q02/p2", "position": "The wording confirms that their ambitions are confined to worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, and Ālūsī say the inserted statement confirms their low aspirations. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says limited knowledge narrows desire, concern, and hope."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q03", "question": "Why is 'their' plural?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q03/p1", "position": "The earlier relative expression is singular in form but denotes a group, so the suffix follows its plural sense.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ālūsī contrast the earlier singular following man in 53:29 with this plural. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the singular verb agrees with man while the plural suffix confirms its group referent."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q04", "question": "Is the limited-knowledge clause parenthetical or the command's direct explanation?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause interrupts a command and its cause or itself supplies that cause.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q04/p1", "position": "It is an interjection or explanatory parenthesis between 'turn away' and the cause given by God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's view is reported by Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Samīn. Al-Samīn argues that an interjection between cause and result is clear, even within a narrative. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it explains ignorance of the afterlife; Bursevī calls it an interruption."}, {"id": "53:30/q04/p2", "position": "It directly explains the command: leave them because this is all they attain.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this, saying their turning away and preference for the immediate explain ignorance. Abū Ḥayyān rejects the aside analysis for lack of basis; al-Samīn reports that objection and answers it."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q05", "question": "Why should the Prophet turn away from these people?", "turns_on": "Whether their resistance, God's judgment, or His knowledge of receptive hearers supplies the immediate emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q05/p1", "position": "Their worldly aims and resistance make further admonition fruitless; his duty of conveying is complete.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says invitations deepen their obstinacy. Al-Kashshāf cites 28:56: the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves. Bursevī and Ālūsī say the persistently astray will not return and he need not exhaust himself. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies Qur'an rejecters through 53:2, 19, 27, 28 and links their withdrawal from remembrance to the command."}, {"id": "53:30/q05/p2", "position": "God knows and will judge both groups, consoling the Prophet and settling their cases.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers three contexts: failed reminders should give way to fighting without uncertainty or despair; opponents claimed guidance despite proof, as in 34:24 and 7:87, so judgment belongs to God; and harm the Prophet endured will be recompensed, as 53:31 indicates. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān call it consolation, warning, and promise. Ibn ʿĀshūr says God's superior knowledge removes grief. Islahi promises no escape for the astray and aid and mercy for the faithful."}, {"id": "53:30/q05/p3", "position": "God alone knows which counsel will work and can bless effective preaching.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says outward worldly knowledge and forceful admonition cannot establish ultimate states. He gives Muṣʿab's preaching: Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh accepted Islam in an hour."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q06", "question": "What does calling God 'your Lord' suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q06/p1", "position": "God's exclusion of an astray person may benefit the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the person might otherwise corrupt more than he improved."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q07", "question": "Does aʿlam mean knowing or knowing better?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is absolute or retains an explicit or implied comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q07/p1", "position": "It may simply mean 'knowing.'", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Rāzī, and Makkī as reported by al-Samīn allow this because God has no equal knower."}, {"id": "53:30/q07/p2", "position": "It may retain the comparative sense: God knows better than any other knower.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās posits an omitted comparison, Rāzī a hypothetical knower, and Makkī allows the comparative. Ibn ʿĀshūr says God knows the people's inner conditions better than the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "53:30/q08", "question": "What is the function of 'He'?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun primarily clarifies syntax or asserts exclusive divine knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "53:30/q08/p1", "position": "It is a separating pronoun clarifying that aʿlam is the predicate.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls it ʿimād or faṣl: the sentence works without it, but a hearer might otherwise take 'most knowing' as part of a following clause."}, {"id": "53:30/q08/p2", "position": "It emphatically restricts hidden knowledge and reckoning to God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says inna and the pronoun emphasize implied reckoning rather than bare omniscience; real restriction excludes the Prophet's knowledge of inner states and relieves his grief."}]}

{"id": "53:33/q09", "question": "How does this passage fit the surrounding argument of the sūra?", "turns_on": "The commentators connect the example to different surrounding themes: recompense, the scriptural case for personal responsibility, ancestral pride, parallels elsewhere, or the sūra's recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:33/q09/p1", "position": "It moves from God's knowledge and recompense to a pointed example of one person's mistaken conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the passage singles out one idolater after exposing the idolaters' ignorance.
